earlier_scan.source_named: Evans et al. 2018, The Languages of Southern New Guinea (in Palmer ed., The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area, De Gruyter) — paywalled

sources.citation: Siegel, Jeff. 2023. A grammar of Nama: a Papuan language of Southern New Guinea (Pacific Linguistics 668). Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.4.3 Stress, pp. 46-47, Table 2.21.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Nama is Dre's only sister in the Nama-Dre subgroup; its stress section is the closest full description and may mention Dre in the introduction or comparative notes.

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas. 2021. The phonetics of Papuan languages in Southern New Guinea: an overview. In Kate L. Lindsey & Dineke Schokkin (eds), Phonetic fieldwork in Southern New Guinea (Language Documentation & Conservation Special Publication 24), 1-?. hdl:10125/24991
sources.note: Regional statement only, p. 7 (p. 3): 'it is difficult to identify any typological features of the phonologies of Southern New Guinea, other than absences (e.g., no tone, no pitch accent or distinctive stress except for Urama, no ejectives etc.)'. Dre is not named anywhere in the chapter; the sample is Nmbo, Nen, Ende, Idi, Bitur, Urama, Yelmek (+ others).
Nothing on phonology; only 'As of 2017, only one elderly speaker remained in the village of Ramar', citing Palmer (ed.) 2017/2018 pp. 681-683.

sources.citation: Carroll, Matthew J. 2020. The morphology of Yam languages. Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics. doi:10.1093/acrefore/9780199384655.013.677 (ANU accepted manuscript, hdl:1885/220610, 74 pp.)
sources.note: Silent. Sections 1-8 are morphology only; no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent', 'prosod' or 'syllable' in the text. Contains Dre data in the case, number, undergoer-prefix and actor-suffix tables (all credited to Evans et al. 2017/2018); Table 2: 'Dre | Ndre | 1 (extinct) | Evans et al. (2017)'; notes speakers shifted 'to another local language, as in Ndre'.

sources.citation: Kashima, Eri. 2020. Language in my mouth: linguistic variation in the Nmbo speech community of Southern New Guinea. PhD thesis, Australian National University. hdl:1885/201927
sources.note: Nothing on Dre stress. p. 48 only locates it: 'the nearly extinct Ndre spoken around Arammba (Tonda branch) territory just south of the Suki.. speaking area' (citing Evans, Arka et al. 2018). For the sister Nambu language Nmbo, p. 109: 'Nmbo stress is obligatory, and tends to fall on the penultimate syllable.'

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas & Julia Colleen Miller. 2016. Nen. Journal of the IPA 46(3): 331-349. doi:10.1017/S0025100315000365
sources.note: Nen (a different Nambu language) only: stress section pp. 343-348, 'basic' first-syllable stress pattern in nouns, word-class- and root-conditioned in verbs. Dre not mentioned.

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas. 2012. Even more diverse than we had thought: the multiplicity of Trans-Fly languages. In Nicholas Evans & Marian Klamer (eds), Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia: challenges for the 21st century (LD&C Special Publication 5), 109-149. hdl:10125/4562
sources.note: Dre/Ndre not mentioned (predates its identification); no stress statement for any Yam language.

sources.citation: Rueck, Michael J. 2011. The Nambu subfamily of the Morehead and Upper Maro Rivers languages: a sociolinguistic survey. SIL Electronic Survey Report (SIL PNG).
